                    ### Question
                    A 24-year-old previously healthy man comes to his physician because of dyspnea and hemoptysis for the past week. Examination shows inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. His hemoglobin concentration is 14.2 g/dL, leukocyte count is 10,300/mm3, and platelet count is 205,000/mm3. Urine dipstick shows 2+ proteins. Urinalysis shows 80 RBC/hpf and 1–2 WBC/hpf. An x-ray of the chest shows pulmonary infiltrates. Further evaluation is most likely to show increased serum titers of which of the following?

                    ### Options

opb. Anti-GBM antibody
opc. Anti-dsDNA antibody
opd. Anti-PLA2R antibody
ope. P-ANCA

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of a 24-year-old man with dyspnea, hemoptysis, inspiratory crackles, hematuria, proteinuria, and pulmonary infiltrates is suggestive of Goodpasture syndrome, an autoimmune condition characterized by the presence of anti-glomerular basement membrane (Anti-GBM) antibodies. The combination of respiratory symptoms and renal involvement aligns with this diagnosis. The reasoning chains indicating increased serum titers of Anti-GBM antibody are supported by the evidence of glomerulonephritis and lung involvement, which are hallmark features of this condition. Other options, such as Anti-dsDNA and P-ANCA, are less likely given the specific symptoms and findings. Therefore, the most likely increased serum titers in this case would be of Anti-GBM antibody.
